units: the writer sends his message straight after a training session
he used to believe the two disciplines called for identical abilities
both practices demand holding a steady rhythm
the burning breath of the first minutes turns up in both activities
when running, the joints absorb the impacts against the ground
when swimming, the sense of weight fades away
the runner's obstacle is the slope of the ground
the swimmer's obstacle is the resistance of the water
alternating the two practices has eased the writer's joint aches
the writer invites his correspondent to try it for himself
text: I am writing with my hair still wet, straight off the back of a session, because something I had wrong for a very long while has finally come clear. For years I lumped running and swimming together, sure they asked for the same qualities. They do share one thing. Both make you hold a steady rhythm, and both begin with that raw burning in the chest until the breath settles down. After that they part company. On the road my joints take every landing, shock upon shock. In the pool my weight simply melts away, leaving nothing but the pull of the shoulders. The runner's adversary is the gradient of the ground; the swimmer's is the water pushing back at him. Since I started swapping one for the other, the old aches in my knees have gone quiet. Give it a go yourself, and write back to tell me how it feels on you.

units: the text answers the questions beginners ask most often
the warm-up must mobilise the ankle and the hip
expensive shoes are not necessary
a sole that grips guards against slipping on wet ground
the breathlessness of the opening minutes clears on its own
a sharp pain signals damaged tissue
muscle repair happens during rest
outings should be lengthened in small weekly steps
the pace chosen must leave room for conversation
text: So you want to move about considerably more without wrecking a knee in the process. The same handful of questions come round week after week, so here they are, in order. Do I need to warm up? Yes, and not with a token wiggle either: the ankle and the hip want waking properly before you set off. Do I need pricey shoes? No. You do need a sole that grips, though, or the first wet pavement will have you over and your ankle with it. Should it hurt? Never. The breathlessness of the opening minutes clears on its own; a sharp, stabbing pain is telling you something has been torn. Should I train flat out every day? No: muscle rebuilds itself while you rest, not while you labour. And how do I get better? Lengthen the outing slightly each week, and hold a pace you could still chat through.

units: the coach breaks the race down into three passages
the favourite set off at an excessive pace
the chasing group let the favourite go without reacting
the turn came on the steep climb of the second lap
the coach's runner passed her rivals one by one
the chaser went into the lead at the top of the climb
she opened up a gap on the downhill section
she accepted a slide in a muddy bend that the others refused
she broke clear of her last rival in the closing stretch
the coach puts the win down to composure rather than power
text: The coach we caught up with just past the finish breaks the race into three passages. At the start, as she tells it, the favourite went off far too hard, and the chasing group let her go without so much as a flicker. Then, on the steep climb of the second lap, the whole thing turned over. “I watched my runner pick them off one by one, and I knew she would close on her,” she says. Her athlete came over the top of the climb in front, then stretched the gap on the way down, where the others were braking out of caution. “She let herself slide through that muddy bend. The rest would not,” the coach adds. Along the closing straight the young woman broke clear of her last rival, with the crowd roaring her home. “She did not win on strength. She won on nerve,” she finishes, her voice catching a little.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: running was first of all an obligation tied to survival
it served to chase game, to carry news or to escape a threat
the reliance on stamina favoured limbs able to hold a lasting pace
that constraint shaped a springy cord at the heel
it also produced abundant sweating
a ligament keeps the neck steady during the stride
the spread of settlements and beasts of burden cut that need back
effort then turned into a measured and rewarded display
our bodies keep the imprint of a use that has become pointless
text: In the earliest days, running was no pastime at all but a plain duty: you ran to bring down an animal, to carry word across country, to get clear of something dangerous. Because survival hung on staying power, human groups kept, without ever choosing to, legs able to hold a modest pace over enormous ground. Out of that need came an odd build, with a springy cord at the heel, a skin that sweats freely, and a slender ligament holding the neck steady stride after stride. Then the settlements spread, roads opened, beasts of burden took up our loads, and the need for running drained away. Effort turned instead into a display: we began to measure it, to compare it, to crown it. That turn of events explains a small strangeness. Our flesh still carries the mark of a use that our lives no longer ask of it.

units: the pain in the side under effort brings many outings to an end
a sheet of muscle divides the chest from the belly
that sheet drives the movement of air in the lungs
short hurried breathing stops it from letting go completely
its prolonged contraction drags on the points where it is anchored
the pain shows up mainly under the ribs on the right side
easing the pace and drawing out the breath is the first remedy
pressing the sore spot while leaning the trunk forwards slackens the anchorage
a heavy meal before setting off encourages the problem to appear
text: A stitch in the side puts an end to more outings than anything else, and its workings are far less mysterious than they look. Below the lungs a sheet of muscle divides the chest from the belly, and it is this sheet that pumps the air. When breathing turns short and hurried, the sheet never lets go completely; it stays contracted and begins to drag on the points where it is anchored. The pain then shows up under the ribs, most often on the right. Three simple corrections settle the matter in nearly every case. First, ease off the pace and draw the breath out long, blowing steadily as the foot opposite the pain lands. Next, press a hand into the sore spot and lean the trunk forwards, which slackens the anchorage. Last, keep off a heavy meal beforehand, since a full stomach shoves the sheet upwards.

units: the sportswoman interviewed now plays in goal
she had begun her career in an attacking position
it took her seasons to see how far apart the two jobs are
the forward moves towards the open spaces
the forward has to forget her failures at once
the keeper falls back towards her goal
the keeper must hold on to every detail because her mistakes are paid for immediately
in her first match in goal she turned away a low shot
the crowd rose to its feet after that save
she holds that the two positions ask for equal courage
text: A goalkeeper once told me a memory of hers that lights up her whole trade. She had begun her career up front, and it took her several seasons to see that the two positions obey opposite logic. A forward, she explained, moves towards the open space: she must spring at the right instant, slip past a defender, and forget her failures immediately. The keeper falls back towards her goal, and must instead hold on to every detail, because a botched move there is paid for at once. On the evening of her first match in goal she dived at a low shot and turned it away with her wrist. The entire crowd rose to their feet. She understood then what attacking had never given her: the thanks of a side for an act of defence. Since that night she has maintained that both roles demand identical courage.

units: preparing a session runs through four successive stages
the first stage covers the kit and its condition
a seam that rubs or careless lacing brings on a skin injury
the second stage is getting the body going
getting going combines brisk walking, joint rotations and short bursts of speed
the third stage alternates fast stretches and calm ones
the pace chosen must stay bearable without clamping the breathing
the fourth stage means coming back down, drinking and stretching the legs
writing down the tiredness felt in a notebook records the progress made
text: Build your session in four stages, and keep them in this order. Stage one is the kit and the state it is in. Check the lacing, check that the sole is still sound, and feel round for any seam that rubs, because a blister grows out of some neglected detail. Stage two is getting the body going. Walk briskly, roll the joints of the legs through their range, then finish with a few short bursts of speed before you truly set off. Stage three is the body of the work: fast stretches alternating with calm ones, at a pace you can carry without clamping down on your breathing. Stage four is coming back down. Slow down in stages, drink, then stretch the thigh and the calf smoothly, without jerking. Finally, record in a notebook how tired you felt: week by week that trace will tell you whether you are progressing.

units: rain was falling as the first competitor reached the platform
there were fears the competition would be called off
the wind dropping left the surface of the water still
the organisers then sent off the opening rounds
the swimmer who opened entered the water with almost no splash
the strictest judge gave her a high mark
one competitor skidded on the wet board and chose to pull out
the equipment was wiped down before the restart
the reigning champion brought off a figure never seen at this venue
she finished ahead of the whole field
text: The rain was already coming down when the first competitor climbed onto the platform, and we were honestly wondering whether the thing would go ahead at all. It did. The wind dropped, the water went flat as a mirror, and the organisers sent off the opening rounds. The first dive caught the crowd cold: she went in with barely a splash, and the strictest judge on the panel handed her a high mark. After that it got messy. One competitor skidded on the soaking board, saved himself at the last moment and chose to pull out. The board was wiped down from end to end, and we carried on. Near the end, the reigning champion tried a figure nobody had dared here, a tucked reversal, and she brought it off. Climbing out of the pool she was still laughing: she had just left the whole of the field behind her.

units: a smell of resin and chalk meets the visitor at the door
the climbing wall takes up the full height of the building
the coloured holds trace routes that are hard to read
thick mats cover the floor and smother the noise of falls
nothing is heard but rubber squeaking and the breathing of the climbers
the openings are kept shut to stop the fingers growing cold
keeping the openings shut sends the heat up inside the room
a teenager hesitates then throws herself at a distant hold
her foot skids and the rope catches her halfway up
it is the repeating of the attempts that brings the progress
text: The smell of resin and chalk takes hold of you the very moment you step in through the door. The climbing wall runs the full height of the building, and its coloured holds trace routes the eye follows without ever quite reading them. Because thick mats swallow the floor, a fall makes no noise at all: you hear nothing but rubber squeaking and climbers breathing. The openings are kept shut, to hold off the draughts that chill the fingers, and so the heat builds inside. At the foot of the wall a teenager hesitates a moment, then throws herself at a hold set far out of reach. Her foot skids, she swings round, and the rope catches her halfway up. She comes back down, blows on her palms, and sets off again. It is out of that endless repeating of the attempt, and out of nothing else, that progress comes.

units: the writer holds it wrong to file movement away among amusements
children now spend their afternoons sitting in front of a screen
that stillness tells on the skeleton, the eyesight and the sleep
blaming families is judged convenient and unjust
the streets have closed themselves to play
the yards of teaching establishments have shrunk in size
the adult timetable leaves no free gap at all
the writer calls for places where noise and falling are tolerated
he suggests opening the covered yards outside teaching hours
he argues that physical tiredness is the mark of a life being used
text: We have filed movement away under amusements, and the filing has cost us dearly. The child who used to climb and jump and roll down a bank now spends the afternoon sitting, a screen within reach. The skeleton suffers for it, the eyesight too, and the sleep most of all. Blaming families comes easily, which is exactly what makes it unjust: the street has closed itself to play, the yards of our teaching places have shrunk, and the adult timetable leaves not a single gap. The way out asks for no great budget and no untried doctrine. Give children back places where noise and falling are tolerated. Open the covered yards outside teaching hours. Accept that a journey made on foot beats a parking space won. And stop treating physical tiredness as a mishap: it is the mark of a life being used.
